title: The Promised Land
aka: from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates
lead: The land of Canaan, promised by God to Abraham and his offspring (Genesis 12:7; 15:18–21) and entered under Joshua. The prophets tie life in the land to faithfulness, and the New Testament widens the promise to the whole world and a heavenly homeland (Romans 4:13; Hebrews 11:13–16).

sections.b: Moses dies looking at the land (Deuteronomy 34:1–4), and Joshua leads Israel in and divides it among the tribes (Joshua 1–21), though much remains unconquered (Judges 1). The land belongs to God, and Israel lives on it as his tenants (Leviticus 25:23). The prophets warn that injustice and idolatry will make the land throw its people out, and Israel and Judah go into exile (2 Kings 17; 25); they also promise a return and a renewed land (Jeremiah 32:36–44; Ezekiel 36:24–28), which begins under Cyrus (Ezra 1). Jesus says the meek will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5), and Paul says Abraham was promised the world (Romans 4:13).
sections.refs: Leviticus 25:23; Deuteronomy 34:1–4; Joshua 1:1–6; Judges 1:1–36; 2 Kings 17:6–23; Jeremiah 32:36–44; Ezekiel 36:24–28; Ezra 1:1–4; Matthew 5:5; Romans 4:13; Hebrews 11:13–16

sections.h: The land in later Jewish and Christian thought
sections.b: For rabbinic Judaism, living in the land of Israel is itself a commandment for many authorities, and the prayers ask daily for the return to Zion. Modern Zionism drew on these hopes, and Jews, Christians and Muslims today read the promise to Abraham in sharply different ways. Many Christians read the land as fulfilled in Christ and the new creation; others, especially dispensationalists, expect its promises to be kept to the Jewish people in history.
